newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin backs Russian defence minister over reform.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin backs Russian defence minister over reform.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, moving freely and with renewed vigour, told his defence minister on Monday he firmly backed his efforts to improve the state of Russia's impoverished armed forces.

Looking healthier than at any time since he fell ill with pneumonia last month, and flashing a broad smile several times, Yeltsin told Defence Minister Igor Rodionov he should feel safe about his job despite speculation that he could be fired.

"Talk, which is heard all the more often of late, about the removal of the defence minister has no basis in truth. This I say as the commander in chief and as president of the Russian Federation," Yeltsin said in Russian television footage.
"There will be no reshuffle in the foreseeable future, that's it."
Rodionov has issued dire warnings about the decrepit state of the once-mighty Russian military, and cautioned that the ability to control its nuclear forces could be in question.

"Yes, today there are big difficulties in the armed forces, and we must give the minister of defence very many powers to correct the situation," Yeltsin said, addressing television cameras as their meeting began.

After the 40-minute encounter, Radionov said he was impressed by Yeltsin's physical appearance more than five weeks after the Russian leader developed pneumonia in both lungs, only two months after undergoing heart surgery.
"I am very glad to see him in good condition, and one feels that the president is gathering strength and health," Rodionov told Russian public television.
Yeltsin also met Andrei Nikolayev, head of Russian border guards, in the latest of a series of meetings with his security chiefs since he began his recovery from pneumonia.

Yeltsin looked thin, but spoke clearly and moved smoothly. Other recent pictures have done little to ease concern over his ability to govern which has prompted his political opponents to seek his removal for health reasons.

Yeltisn, 66, acknowledged that Rodionov had clashed over reforms with Yuri Baturin, secretary of the president's advisory Defence Council and long-term Yeltsin ally, but the president said he welcomed differing views.

"Yes, there have been some differences between Rodionov and Baturin on military reform," he said. "Of course there can be different opinions -- then the president will decide conclusively which point of view to choose."
Rodionov "constantly reports to me, informs me on the state of matters in the military and the difficulties they are having, and I try to help him," Yeltsin said.

Rodionov, 60, who recently left the army to become Russia's first civilian defence minister, has been fighting a loud campaign for support and funds for the military and had to write a letter to Yeltsin before being granted a meeting.
His warnings were reinforced on Friday when a non-government research group said the military is in such shambles that it could collapse, prompting a military coup or civil war.

"Not only did the president not show mistrust in us, he also shared our worries and concern. He supported us in the idea that, regardless of the acute situation and under all circumstances, the truth has to be told," Rodionov told Interfax news agency after the meeing.
For several years the Russian leadership has expressed its intention of launching sweeping military reforms, but differences among the top brass have prevented them from making progress.
During his re-election campaign last year, Yeltsin promised to replace Russia's conscript army with a professional force by 2000, but both Rodionov and Baturin say Russia cannot meet this goal.
